facts.text: The WTaVTi precursor underwent liquid-metal dealloying by immersion in molten Cu to selectively replace its Ti-rich interdendritic regions with Cu.
The precursor and Cu were vacuum-sealed in silica and reacted at 1200 °C for 96 h.
Helium screening used 25 keV He+ implantation to fluences near 8–8.5 × 10^17 atoms cm−2 and was performed on precursor dendrites as a proxy for RHEA ligaments, not on the finished composite.
Dealloying produced a directionally aligned bicontinuous structure containing approximately 63.6 vol.% BCC RHEA ligaments and 36.4 vol.% nearly pure FCC Cu channels.
An approximately 300 nm W-rich interlayer formed spontaneously at each RHEA/Cu interface.
Ti preferentially exchanged with and dissolved into molten Cu, whereas the comparatively Cu-immiscible W, Ta, and V remained as continuous RHEA ligaments.
Continued Ti extraction left W trapped at the interface, forming a passivating W-rich layer that arrested further exchange and stabilized RHEA/Cu bonding.

The aligned Cu channels supplied conductive pathways, while the positive temperature dependence of conductivity was attributed to reduced diffuse interfacial mismatch and increasing lattice-mediated transport.
The dealloyed composite had substantially higher thermal conductivity than the unprocessed WTaVTi precursor and surpassed pure W at approximately 650 °C.
At room temperature, the composite thermal conductivity was approximately 75 W m−1 K−1, about 4.4 times the precursor value of approximately 17 W m−1 K−1.
Under 25 keV He+ irradiation, WTaVTi dendrites showed lower swelling and later blistering/cracking than pure W.
At blistering, WTaVTi swelling was approximately 108% versus approximately 137% for pure W, corresponding to about 30% lower swelling.
